insights.title: Your genes mean clopidogrel may work less well for you
insights.found: Your CYP2C19 result is *2/*2, a poor metaboliser. You take clopidogrel 75 mg after your heart stent (12 months planned).
insights.why: Clopidogrel is activated by the CYP2C19 enzyme, and the CPIC guideline is level A for this gene and medicine.
insights.means: In poor metabolisers on clopidogrel after a stent, the guideline says to consider another antiplatelet medicine, such as prasugrel or ticagrelor, where it is safe. You also take warfarin, so the choice is your cardiologist's.
insights.do: Do not stop clopidogrel. Show this result to your cardiologist soon.
insights.expected: A decision that fits your genes and your other medicines.
insights.helps: The most important result in your record.

insights.title: Your genes and your muscle aches both point at simvastatin
insights.found: Your SLCO1B1 result is *1/*5 (decreased function). You take simvastatin 40 mg at night and have had mild thigh aches for about 6 weeks. Creatine kinase was 180 U/L, inside the lab's range.
insights.why: The CPIC guideline (level A) links this genotype to statin muscle symptoms.
insights.means: For decreased-function genotypes the guideline says to limit the simvastatin dose or use another statin.
insights.do: Tell your doctor about the aches and this result. Do not stop simvastatin on your own.
insights.expected: A statin and dose that suit your genes.

insights.title: Your genes make you more sensitive to warfarin
insights.found: CYP2C9 *1/*3 and VKORC1 c.-1639G>A A/A. You take warfarin, 4 mg daily adjusted to your INR; your INR was 2.4 (target 2.0-3.0).
insights.why: The CPIC guideline (level A) recommends a genotype-informed dosing method rather than a fixed starting dose.
insights.means: Your current dose is already set by your INR, which is in range. The genotype matters most if warfarin is restarted or other medicines change.
insights.do: Make sure every doctor who changes your medicines knows these results.
insights.expected: Fewer surprises at the next change.

insights.title: Your TSH is mildly raised on levothyroxine
insights.found: TSH 6.8 mIU/L on 10 Oct 2026. You take levothyroxine 50 mcg, and your record lists suspected underactive thyroid caused by amiodarone.
insights.why: Our rule flags a TSH between 4 and 10.
insights.means: The rule says a single value in this band is a weak basis for any change: TSH varies about 18% from day to day. It asks for free T4, free T3 and anti-TPO from the same laboratory. It was written for people not yet on levothyroxine, so it applies to you only in part.
insights.do: Ask your doctor about a repeat thyroid panel from the same lab.
insights.expected: A clearer picture before any dose change.

insights.title: Your 12 medicines need a pharmacist's interaction check
insights.found: You take 12 medicines. Our interaction screen flagged no pair among them.
insights.why: Our screen states that a missing flag means the pair was not screened, not that it is safe: licensed interaction databases are not available to it.
insights.means: The gene results above are checked; drug-to-drug interactions among your 12 medicines are not fully checked.
insights.do: Ask for a full medication review by a pharmacist, bringing this list and your gene results.
insights.expected: Every pair checked by someone with the full databases.

insights.title: Your HbA1c is 7.1%
insights.found: HbA1c 7.1% on 10 Oct 2026. You have type 2 diabetes and take metformin 1000 mg twice daily.
insights.why: Our rule flags HbA1c at or above the diabetes-range criterion.
insights.means: The rule is written for diagnosis; for you it marks where your control stands. Your doctor sets your target.
insights.do: Ask about your HbA1c target; our analysis suggests a repeat within 3 months.
insights.expected: A trend to judge your treatment by.

insights.title: One liver enzyme is above the South Indian healthy range
insights.why: It is above 28 U/L, the 97.5th percentile of healthy South Indian men, though below most labs' upper limit.
insights.means: Our rule reads it with a liver-scarring score and proposes no test on its own.
insights.do: Mention it at your medication review.
insights.expected: Your doctor decides whether to follow it up.

insights.title: Your haemoglobin is slightly below the usual range for men
insights.why: It is below 13.5, the healthy male fifth centile in our rule's source.
insights.means: A population boundary, not a decision point. The question is whether iron is low.
insights.do: Ask whether iron studies are needed.
insights.expected: A cause, if there is one.

insights.title: Your eGFR may overestimate your kidney function
insights.why: In Indian cohorts creatinine-based equations overestimate kidney function in the 60-89 band.
insights.means: Several of your medicines are cleared by the kidneys, so an accurate number matters. Urine albumin has not been measured.
insights.do: Ask about cystatin C and a urine albumin test.

ask.q: What do my genes say about warfarin?
ask.a: CYP2C9 *1/*3 and VKORC1 A/A make you more sensitive to warfarin. Your INR was 2.4, in the 2.0-3.0 target, so your current dose works. The genotype matters at any restart or medicine change.

ask.q: Do my medicines interact with each other?
ask.a: Our screen flagged no pair among your 12 medicines, but it says plainly that this means the pairs were not screened, not that they are safe. Ask a pharmacist for a full review.

Your TSH was 6.8 on levothyroxine 50 mcg, and your record lists suspected underactive thyroid from amiodarone. One value in the 4-10 range is a weak basis for a change; a repeat with free T4, free T3 and anti-TPO from the same lab is the next step.

A targeted panel: CYP2C19 *2/*2 (poor metaboliser), CYP2C9 *1/*3, VKORC1 c.-1639G>A A/A, SLCO1B1 *1/*5 (decreased function) and CYP3A5 *3/*3. Three of these produced guideline findings for medicines you take.
Your HbA1c was 7.1% on metformin. Your doctor sets your target; a repeat within 3 months shows the trend.

ask.q: Are my kidneys OK for my medicines?
ask.a: eGFR 65, and in Indian cohorts this equation tends to read high. Several of your medicines are cleared by the kidneys, so cystatin C and a urine albumin test would help your doctor dose them.

ask.a: It found 25 biological targets (the portal lists the first 12), including your tested genes (CYP2C19, CYP2C9, VKORC1, SLCO1B1, CYP3A5) and statin and blood-pressure targets, and profiled 582 known compounds. No docking was run. Research only.

glossary: Pharmacogenomics (PGx)
How your genes change the way your body handles some medicines.
TSH
Thyroid-stimulating hormone. High means your body wants more thyroid hormone.
HbA1c
Average blood sugar over about the last 2-3 months.
eGFR
Estimated glomerular filtration rate: how well your kidneys filter, calculated from creatinine, age and sex.
ALT
Alanine aminotransferase: a liver enzyme measured in blood.
Haemoglobin
The protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen.
Rule
One of our clinical checks. Each has a source, a threshold and an evidence grade; it fires only when your result clears it.
INR
International normalised ratio: how long your blood takes to clot, used to set the warfarin dose.
CYP2C19
A liver enzyme gene. Poor metabolisers activate clopidogrel less.
SLCO1B1
A gene for a liver transporter. Decreased function raises statin levels in the blood.
CPIC
Clinical Pharmacogenetics Implementation Consortium: publishes gene-medicine guidelines.
